nodes.label: Ubaid Mesopotamia
nodes.full: The pottery-Neolithic and Ubaid centuries that end here — the first settlement of the alluvium, the Eridu temple sequence, the token accounts, the stamp seal and the slow wheel, all of which Uruk scales up. See the folio mesopotamia-6500bc-3800bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio mesopotamia-6500bc-3800bc.

nodes.label: The Uruk periphery
nodes.full: The lands the expansion reached — the middle Euphrates, the Taurus foothills, the Nineveh plain, the Zagros passes — with their own farming societies that hosted, emulated or resisted the southern colonies and returned to local trajectories after the collapse.
nodes.src: background — Algaze, 'The Uruk World System' (2005); Frangipane's Arslantepe work.

nodes.label: Predynastic Egypt
nodes.full: Late Naqada Egypt, which briefly absorbed Mesopotamian motifs and forms — the cylinder seal, the niched facade, the master of animals — into the imagery of its own emerging kingship. See the folio egypt-6000bc-3000bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio egypt-6000bc-3000bc; Toby Wilkinson, 'Early Dynastic Egypt' (1999).

nodes.label: Proto-Elamite Iran
nodes.full: The Iranian plateau's answer to Uruk: around 3100 BC it produced its own accounting script and a network of towns centred on Susa and Anshan, prompted by the Mesopotamian model but developed separately.
nodes.src: background — Robert Englund on Proto-Elamite; Daniel Potts, 'The Archaeology of Elam' (1999).

nodes.label: The Early Dynastic city-states
nodes.full: The age that follows: a dozen walled southern city-states — Ur, Uruk, Lagash, Umma, Kish, Nippur — sharing a script, a pantheon and a language, and fighting one another over land and water. See the folio sumer-2900bc-2334bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio sumer-2900bc-2334bc.

nodes.label: The making of Uruk
nodes.full: Two adjacent settlements — Kullaba around the terrace of the sky-god Anu, and Eanna around the precinct of Inanna — fused and swelled as the villages around them emptied their people into the growing town. By about 3300 BC Uruk covered some 250 hectares behind its wall, holding tens of thousands of people: the largest single settlement anywhere on earth, and the first place that can be called a city.
nodes.src: German Archaeological Institute excavations at Warka since 1912 (Jordan, Heinrich, Lenzen, Nissen, Eichmann); settlement scale in Hans Nissen, 'The Early History of the Ancient Near East' (1988).

nodes.label: Eanna and Kullaba — power as institution
nodes.full: The centre of Uruk was not a palace but a precinct: a shifting complex of vast tripartite halls, colonnades and terraces — the Limestone Temple, the Pillar Hall, the Riemchen Building, the Stone-Cone Temple — repeatedly built, used, demolished and levelled. From the buildings of Eanna came the world's first written archives. Whatever ran Uruk did so through the temple household, not a named king.
nodes.src: Eanna building sequence in Ernst Heinrich, 'Die Tempel und Heiligtümer im alten Mesopotamien' (1982); the administrative context of the archaic texts in Nissen, Damerow & Englund, 'Archaic Bookkeeping' (1993).

nodes.label: The 'priest-king' — a ruler without a name
nodes.full: A single figure recurs on the seals and stone monuments of late Uruk: a bearded man in a netted skirt and rolled headband who feeds the temple flocks, receives the harvest, spears bound prisoners and hunts lions. Modern scholars call him the 'priest-king' or by the later title en. He is an office made visible — the city's leadership shown as one man — but no text gives him a name or a reign.
nodes.src: Iconography analysed in Irene Winter, 'The Uruk Trough' and in Denise Schmandt-Besserat, 'When Writing Met Art' (2007); the office debated in Nissen (1988) and Marc Van De Mieroop, 'A History of the Ancient Near East' (2016).

nodes.label: The Uruk expansion
nodes.full: Southern material culture — bevelled-rim bowls, cylinder seals, numerical tablets, tripartite buildings — appears far from the alluvium: as planned walled towns on the middle Euphrates (Habuba Kabira, Jebel Aruda), as enclaves inside local settlements at the Euphrates bend (Hacınebi), and along the roads east into the Zagros (Godin Tepe, Nineveh, Tepe Sialk). Whether this was a trade diaspora, a colonial project or something in between is still argued.
nodes.src: Guillermo Algaze, 'The Uruk World System' (1993; 2nd ed. 2005); Habuba Kabira in Eva Strommenger, 'Habuba Kabira: Eine Stadt vor 5000 Jahren' (1980).

nodes.label: The collapse of the expansion
nodes.full: Within a few generations the northern colonies were abandoned or burned, and southern goods vanished from the periphery. The Syrian and Anatolian north returned to its own path (the Ninevite 5 culture), and the Iranian plateau turned to its own Proto-Elamite states and script. Uruk the city carried on, larger than ever, but the wide network it had projected was gone.
nodes.src: Reviewed in Algaze (2005) and in Marcella Frangipane, 'The Collapse of the Uruk system' and her Arslantepe work; chronology in Nissen (1988).

nodes.label: The city-seals of the Uruk III period
nodes.full: The transitional 'Jemdet Nasr' period is named for a small mound near Kish. Clay sealings from it and from Ur are impressed with a recurring string of city names — Ur, Uruk, Larsa, Nippur, Kesh, Zabalam, Umma and more — written as a set. Something bound the southern cities together: a rotating obligation to a shared cult, a pool for tribute or defence, a league. The detail is lost; the fact of it is not.
nodes.src: Roger Matthews, 'Cities, Seals and Writing: Archaic Seal Impressions from Jemdet Nasr and Ur' (1993); the site first dug by Ernest Mackay (1926), re-excavated by Matthews (1988–89).

nodes.label: The southern cities take shape
nodes.full: By the close of the period Ur, Nippur, Shuruppak, Eridu, Kish and Uruk were all walled cities with monumental temple precincts and their own growing archives. The political map of the Early Dynastic age — a dozen rival city-states sharing a language, a pantheon and a script — was in place. What came next was the competition between them for land, water and primacy.
nodes.src: Settlement pattern in Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); the transition to Early Dynastic in Jean-Jacques Glassner, 'Mesopotamian Chronicles' and in Van De Mieroop (2016).

nodes.label: War on the seals and the Warka Vase
nodes.full: Late Uruk cylinder seals and stone monuments carry the first sustained images of organised violence in Mesopotamia: the priest-king driving a spear into a kneeling naked captive, files of bound prisoners with arms pinned behind them being beaten, heaps of the slain. War, and the display of victory over other people, is part of what the new institution does and shows.
nodes.src: The 'priest-king' war imagery catalogued in Schmandt-Besserat, 'When Writing Met Art' (2007) and in Zainab Bahrani, 'Rituals of War' (2008).

nodes.label: The wall of Uruk
nodes.full: A brick rampart roughly nine kilometres long, studded with towers, enclosed the whole city — one of the largest construction projects of its age and a statement that Uruk was a thing to be defended and set apart. A thousand years later the Epic of Gilgamesh would open by inviting the reader to walk this wall and admire it, and would name Gilgamesh of Uruk as its builder.
nodes.src: Wall traced by the German expedition (Nissen, Eichmann); the literary memory in Andrew George, 'The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic' (2003), Tablet I.

nodes.label: Habuba Kabira — colony or garrison?
nodes.full: The southern town on the Syrian river was set out in advance on a planned street grid, behind a wall three metres thick with regular towers and two gates, and then occupied — a deliberate, fortified foundation on someone else's river. Whether the Uruk expansion was armed conquest, a chain of gated trading stations, or peaceful settlement among willing hosts is a question the walls of Habuba Kabira keep open.
nodes.src: Kay Kohlmeyer & Eva Strommenger on Habuba Kabira-süd; the interpretive spectrum set out in Gil Stein, 'Rethinking World-Systems' (1999) against Algaze's model.

nodes.label: The burning of the frontier
nodes.full: Several expansion sites end in ash and collapse. It is not clear whether the colonies were stormed by neighbours who had had enough, abandoned in a hurry under pressure, or wound down and torched on departure. The reading matters: a violent end argues that the system was resented and coercive, a quiet one that it was a commercial arrangement that simply stopped paying.
nodes.src: Destruction levels discussed in Frangipane's Arslantepe reports and in Algaze (2005); the coercion debate in Stein (1999).

nodes.label: The birth of writing
nodes.full: From the Eanna archives comes the earliest writing: some five thousand clay tablets and fragments, drawn with a reed in pictures and impressed numbers. About nine in ten are administrative accounts — barley issued, sheep counted, cloth delivered, fields measured, work-gangs fed — and the rest are lists for teaching. It began as a way to record quantities and things, not connected speech, and only over centuries grew into a script that could write sentences.
nodes.src: Hans Nissen, Peter Damerow & Robert Englund, 'Archaic Bookkeeping' (1993); Robert Englund, 'Texts from the Late Uruk Period' (1998); the corpus published in the ATU series and the CDLI.

nodes.label: The bevelled-rim bowl and the ration
nodes.full: Coarse, mould-made bowls of a roughly standard size were turned out and thrown away in the hundreds of thousands across the Uruk world — the commonest object of the period. The written sign for a food ration is a picture of one. They are read as the vessels in which the temple and its offshoots doled out a daily measure of barley or barley porridge to the dependent people who worked for them.
nodes.src: Function argued in Nissen (1988); alternative bread-mould reading in Daniel Potts, 'Bevelled-Rim Bowls and Bakeries' (2009); the ration sign in 'Archaic Bookkeeping' (1993).

nodes.label: The Standard List of Professions
nodes.full: Among the oldest school texts is a fixed list of roughly a hundred and forty titles and occupations, running from the highest offices of the city down through supervisors, priests, craftsmen and herders. Scribes copied it, in the same order, for more than a thousand years. It is the administered hierarchy of the first cities written out as a single document — an org-chart of the world's first bureaucracy.
nodes.src: Edited in Robert Englund & Hans Nissen, 'Die lexikalischen Listen der archaischen Texte aus Uruk' (ATU 3, 1993); its long transmission traced by Niek Veldhuis, 'History of the Cuneiform Lexical Tradition' (2014).

nodes.label: The cylinder seal replaces the stamp
nodes.full: A small stone cylinder engraved in reverse, rolled across wet clay to leave a continuous picture-frieze, took over from the pressed stamp seal. It gave more image, more individuality and more security, and it was used everywhere the administration reached — sealing jars, sacks, bales, storeroom doors and the tablets themselves. The cylinder seal is the Uruk state's signature, and it stays in use for three thousand years.
nodes.src: Pierre Amiet, 'La glyptique mésopotamienne archaïque' (2nd ed. 1980); Rainer Michael Boehmer, 'Uruk: Kleinfunde' (the seal corpus); Holly Pittman on the expansion-period glyptic.

nodes.label: The accounting systems and the standard measure
nodes.full: The archaic scribes ran several separate number systems at once — one for counting discrete things, others for grain capacity, for field area and for calendar time — each with its own signs and its own step-ratios. Fixed units of barley, of land and of the labour day tied every account to a common standard, so that rations, harvests, field sizes and work quotas could all be added and checked.
nodes.src: The parallel metrologies reconstructed in Jöran Friberg's studies and in 'Archaic Bookkeeping' (1993), ch. 3–5.

nodes.label: Inanna of Eanna
nodes.full: The great precinct of Uruk belonged to Inanna — goddess of the storehouse and its overflowing gate, of sexual desire, of war, and of the planet seen as the morning and evening star. Her house, Eanna, 'the house of heaven', was the richest institution in the city. The later Sumerian hymns that make her the most restless and dangerous of the gods are singing about the deity at the centre of the first urban economy.
nodes.src: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'The Treasures of Darkness' (1976), ch. 3; the Eanna cult in the archaic texts (Englund 1998).

nodes.label: The god's household
nodes.full: The theology that organised the first cities was economic: the god owned an estate — fields, orchards, herds of thousands, fishing rights, workshops — and the community existed to work it and be fed from it. The temple was that estate's headquarters. Worship, labour and taxation were not yet separate things; to serve the city was to serve the god's household.
nodes.src: The 'temple-estate' model set out by Anna Schneider and Anton Deimel from the Early Dynastic Lagash texts, and read back onto Uruk; its limits discussed in Benjamin Foster, 'A New Look at the Sumerian Temple State' (1981).

nodes.label: The Warka Vase and the offering
nodes.full: A metre-high alabaster vase carved in three bands: below, the barley and the flocks of the land; above them, a file of naked men carrying baskets and jars of that produce; at the top, the goods heaped in the storehouse before the goddess, with the priest-king approaching. It is the first narrative relief in Mesopotamian art, and it states the whole social contract — the land's yield goes up to the god, and the leader mediates.
nodes.src: Julius Jordan's 1934 find; iconography in Zainab Bahrani and in Claudia Suter, 'The Uruk Vase' studies; looted and partly recovered from the Iraq Museum in 2003.

nodes.label: The high terrace of Anu
nodes.full: On the Kullaba side of Uruk, the sky-god Anu's shrine sat on a steep mud-brick platform twelve metres high, its small tripartite temple whitewashed brilliant against the plain — the 'White Temple'. Raising the god's house above the city on an artificial mountain is the idea that grows, over the next fifteen hundred years, into the stepped ziggurat.
nodes.src: Ernst Heinrich, 'Die Tempel und Heiligtümer im alten Mesopotamien' (1982); recent re-analysis by the DAI Uruk project (Margarete van Ess, Ricardo Eichmann).

nodes.label: The cone-mosaic facade
nodes.full: The columns and walls of the Eanna courtyards were sheathed in tens of thousands of small baked-clay cones, their flat ends dipped in black, red and buff paint and pressed point-first into thick mud plaster to make bands, zigzags and lozenges of colour. It was an enormous investment of labour to give the goddess's house a dazzling, weatherproof, permanent skin.
nodes.src: Cone mosaics from the Eanna 'Pillar Hall' and 'Cone-Mosaic Courtyard', published in the Uruk excavation reports (UVB series); overview in Heinrich (1982).

nodes.label: The Mask of Warka
nodes.full: A life-size face carved from white marble — brows and large eyes once inlaid with shell and coloured stone, the hair a separate gold or copper cap now lost — probably the cult image of Inanna or a votive head fixed to a wooden body. It is one of the earliest attempts anywhere to model a specific human face in the round, and its calm frontality sets the pattern for Mesopotamian sculpture. Stolen from the Iraq Museum in 2003 and recovered months later.
nodes.src: Found by Julius Jordan (1939); studied in Zainab Bahrani, 'The Infinite Image' (2014); 2003 theft and recovery documented by the Iraq Museum and the FBI Art Crime Team.

nodes.label: The Uruk Trough
nodes.full: A gypsum water trough carved along both faces with a file of rams and ewes moving toward a reed byre, from whose door lambs step out, framed by the looped reed ring-posts that stand for Inanna. It is a pastoral scene — the flock, the fold, the increase — turned into a temple object, celebrating the herd on which the goddess's wealth and the city's food depended.
nodes.src: British Museum collection; discussed in Julian Reade, 'Early Mesopotamia' and in Bahrani, 'The Infinite Image' (2014).

nodes.label: The Lion-Hunt Stele and monumental relief
nodes.full: A slab of black basalt shows the priest-king twice over — thrusting a spear into a lion and loosing an arrow into another — the earliest freestanding carved monument from Mesopotamia. With the period's stone animals in the round, it begins the long Mesopotamian tradition of public relief in which the ruler proves his fitness by mastering beasts and enemies.
nodes.src: Iraq Museum; Rainer Michael Boehmer on the Uruk stone monuments; the hunt-as-legitimation theme in Bahrani, 'Rituals of War' (2008).

nodes.label: The priest-king cycle on the seals
nodes.full: The finest late-Uruk cylinder seals return again and again to the same handful of scenes: the priest-king feeding the temple herd, receiving the harvest, sailing in a high-prowed boat with the goddess's emblem, and spearing captives. Rolled out on jar-stoppers and door-sealings all over the city, this small repeated repertoire is a coordinated image of who holds authority and why — political art at the scale of a thumbnail.
nodes.src: Pierre Amiet, 'La glyptique mésopotamienne archaïque' (1980); Denise Schmandt-Besserat, 'When Writing Met Art' (2007).

nodes.label: The pot gives way to the seal and the wall
nodes.full: The painted-pottery traditions that had carried Mesopotamian visual art for two thousand years ended here: Uruk pottery is plain, fast, wheel-made and made to be used and discarded. The care and the meaning moved elsewhere — onto the engraved seal, the carved stone vessel and statue, and the vast coloured, recessed facades of the temple. Art became monumental and institutional as the city rose.
nodes.src: The shift discussed in Hans Nissen (1988) and in Bahrani, 'The Infinite Image' (2014).

nodes.label: The lyre enters the record
nodes.full: The archaic sign lists include BALAG, the word that later means both a stringed instrument and a class of lament-hymn, and late-Uruk seals show seated figures playing what appears to be a bull-fronted lyre. The temple musician and the sung lament — offices and forms attested in full detail a few centuries later at Ur — have their first faint traces in the Uruk material.
nodes.src: The BALAG sign in the archaic lexical lists (Englund & Nissen 1993); lyre iconography in Theo Krispijn, 'The Uruk archaic lyre' studies; continuity with the Ur lyres in Anne Kilmer's work.

nodes.label: A sign for a thing, not yet for a word
nodes.full: The first script could record that thirty-three measures of barley went to a named official over a stated period — but it could not yet write 'the official said' or 'the barley was stolen'. Its signs stood for objects, quantities and a small set of institutional relations, arranged in boxes on the tablet, not in the order of speech. Turning this accounting device into a full writing of language took another five hundred years.
nodes.src: Peter Damerow, 'The Origins of Writing as a Problem of Historical Epistemology' (2006); Jean-Jacques Glassner, 'The Invention of Cuneiform' (2003).

nodes.label: The lexical lists
nodes.full: Alongside the accounts, Uruk scribes copied lists that classified the world: kinds of trees and wooden objects, of vessels, of animals, of cities, of officials. These were teaching texts, but they were also the first sustained attempt to sort reality into ordered categories and fix the order in writing — the root of a Mesopotamian intellectual habit, list-making as a way of knowing, that runs for three millennia.
nodes.src: Niek Veldhuis, 'History of the Cuneiform Lexical Tradition' (2014); the archaic lists edited in Englund & Nissen, ATU 3 (1993).

nodes.label: Field area and the reckoning of quantity
nodes.full: The archaic accounts already compute: they add and subdivide grain measures, work out the area of fields from their sides, convert between a labour quota and the barley to pay it, and balance what came in against what went out. The distinct systems of signs, and the step-ratios between units, contain the seeds of the sexagesimal mathematics that later Babylonian scribes would develop into something powerful.
nodes.src: Jöran Friberg's analyses of the archaic metrological and 'field-plan' texts; overview in 'Archaic Bookkeeping' (1993) and in Eleanor Robson, 'Mathematics in Ancient Iraq' (2008).

nodes.label: The administrative year
nodes.full: To schedule rations, rents and deliveries, the Uruk administration kept a formal calendar — a year of twelve months of thirty ideal days, with the discrepancy against the real lunar and solar year quietly absorbed. It is an accountant's time, imposed for control rather than derived from the sky, and it sits underneath every dated account in the archive.
nodes.src: Robert Englund, 'Administrative Timekeeping in Ancient Mesopotamia' (JESHO 1988); the later cultic calendars in Mark Cohen, 'The Cultic Calendars of the Ancient Near East' (1993).

nodes.label: The temple estate as an enterprise
nodes.full: The Eanna archives show a single institution running the economy at a scale no household could: field teams working hundreds of hectares, herds of tens of thousands of sheep and goats, textile and food workshops, fishing and fowling crews, and the scribes and overseers to account for all of it. Production, storage and redistribution were centralised in the god's house, and most of the city's people worked within that system.
nodes.src: Josef Bauer, Robert Englund & Manfred Krebernik, 'Mesopotamien: Späturuk-Zeit und Frühdynastische Zeit' (1998); Benjamin Foster, 'A New Look at the Sumerian Temple State' (1981).

nodes.label: Rationed labour and the unfree worker
nodes.full: Much of the work was done by gangs of dependent labourers — men and women listed by name and fed a fixed daily measure of barley from bevelled-rim bowls. The archaic sign for a female captive combines the signs for 'woman' and 'mountain': the unfree came from the highlands, taken in the raids the priest-king is shown conducting. The first cities ran on managed, rationed and partly coerced labour.
nodes.src: Ignace Gelb, 'Prisoners of War in Early Mesopotamia' (JNES 1973); labour organisation in 'Archaic Bookkeeping' (1993) and Robert Englund's Ur III studies read back onto Uruk.

nodes.label: Wool and the textile workshop
nodes.full: Uruk was a cloth factory. Enormous flocks were kept primarily for wool; the archaic accounts track fleece by weight and finished textiles by type; and the spinning and weaving were done by large workforces of women and children attached to the institutions. Cloth was the manufactured good the resource-poor south could export in bulk to pay for the metal, stone and timber it had to import.
nodes.src: Wool and textile accounts in Englund (1998); the wider process in Joy McCorriston, 'The Fiber Revolution' (Current Anthropology 1997).

nodes.label: Cereal farming at scale — and the first salt
nodes.full: Feeding a city meant farming in large blocks: long strip-fields ploughed and sown by teams, planted mostly to barley, with fallow and rotation planned centrally. Watering land year after year in a hot climate with poor drainage began to draw salt up into the topsoil — a slow poisoning of the southern fields that the records hint at here and that later becomes a recurring Mesopotamian crisis.
nodes.src: Thorkild Jacobsen & Robert Adams, 'Salt and Silt in Ancient Mesopotamian Agriculture' (Science 1958); field organisation in Jöran Friberg's 'field-plan' text studies.

nodes.label: Full-time specialists
nodes.full: The Standard List of Professions names them: potters throwing on the fast wheel, smiths, seal-cutters, stone-carvers, carpenters, leather-workers, brewers, cooks. In a city fed from a central store, these people could work their craft full time and be paid in rations. Deep specialisation — the potter who only pots — is one of the things that makes a city more productive than the sum of its villages.
nodes.src: Occupations in the Standard List of Professions (Englund & Nissen 1993); craft organisation surveyed in Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994).

nodes.label: The expansion as an economy
nodes.full: On one influential reading, the whole Uruk expansion was the alluvium's economy reaching outward for what it lacked — copper, silver, lead, tin, timber, building stone, semiprecious stone — by planting trading stations on the routes that carried them. At Godin Tepe an oval walled compound held Uruk-style tablets, seals and storage jars whose residues include the earliest chemically identified wine and barley beer.
nodes.src: Guillermo Algaze, 'Ancient Mesopotamia at the Dawn of Civilization' (2008); Godin Tepe in Gopnik & Rothman (eds.), 'On the High Road' (2011); residues in Patrick McGovern's analyses.

nodes.label: The fast wheel and the mass-produced bowl
nodes.full: Uruk potters worked on a true fast wheel, throwing vessels from a spinning lump in minutes, and turned out the ubiquitous ration bowl by pressing clay into a mould. Pottery went from a craft to an industry — fast, uniform, cheap and disposable — the first mass production, and the technology that made a citywide ration system physically possible.
nodes.src: Wheel-throwing evidence in Valentine Roux's technological studies; production scale in Hans Nissen (1988).

nodes.label: The wheel and the wagon
nodes.full: The archaic sign lists include a pictograph of a wheeled sledge, and within a few generations one of a four-wheeled wagon. Mesopotamia in the late Uruk period is one of the two or three regions where the wheel-and-axle first appears, alongside the northern Black Sea steppe and central Europe. Solid disc wheels on ox-drawn wagons and sledges moved bulk goods that boats could not reach.
nodes.src: The GIGIR pictograph in the archaic texts; near-simultaneous first evidence across Eurasia reviewed in Bakker et al., 'The earliest evidence of wheeled vehicles' (Antiquity 1999).

nodes.label: The reed stylus and the clay tablet
nodes.full: The medium was the cheapest thing in Mesopotamia: a lump of river clay patted into a pillow-shaped tablet, written on with the cut end of a reed, and either baked or simply left to harden. Early scribes drew curved pictographs; pressing the reed instead of dragging it turned every stroke into a wedge, faster to make and the reason the script is called cuneiform.
nodes.src: Materiality of the tablet in Jean-Jacques Glassner, 'The Invention of Cuneiform' (2003); the pictograph-to-wedge shift in Christopher Woods (ed.), 'Visible Language' (2010).

nodes.label: The seeder-plough
nodes.full: Mesopotamian farmers fitted the ard plough with an upright funnel through which a second worker trickled seed straight into the fresh furrow as the ox team walked. Sowing and covering the seed in one pass saved grain and labour and gave even, deep planting. Shown on Uruk seals and standard on the alluvium ever after, the seeder-plough was one of the region's most durable inventions.
nodes.src: Seeder-plough on late-Uruk glyptic (Amiet 1980); agricultural technology in Armas Salonen, 'Agricultura Mesopotamica' (1968).

nodes.label: Casting scales up
nodes.full: Metalwork grew from beads and pins to cast tools, weapons, vessels and figurines, worked in copper deliberately alloyed with arsenic for hardness and cast in open and two-piece moulds, with lost-wax casting for complex shapes. The ore and metal all came from outside — one of the strongest reasons the cities pushed their reach toward the highlands.
nodes.src: Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994); arsenical-copper metallurgy in Thilo Rehren and in Christopher Thornton's surveys of the Iranian sources.

nodes.label: Monumental brick construction
nodes.full: The Eanna precinct demanded engineering: small squared 'Riemchen' bricks laid in the millions, artificial terraces raised and revetted, ramps and stairs, drains and water-channels within the sanctuary, walls decorated with inset cone mosaic and niched to relieve their mass. Building at this scale needed a workforce fed and directed by an institution — architecture and administration grew up together.
nodes.src: Ernst Heinrich, 'Die Tempel und Heiligtümer im alten Mesopotamien' (1982); the Eanna building techniques in the German excavation reports (UVB / Baghdader Mitteilungen).

nodes.label: A core and its periphery
nodes.full: On Guillermo Algaze's model, the Uruk cities formed the first 'world system': a resource-rich but raw-material-poor core on the alluvium, drawing metal, stone and timber from a highland and riverine periphery through colonies, trade enclaves and the emulation of its prestige goods. Critics answer that the periphery had its own complex societies and agency, and was not simply worked by the south — the debate has run for thirty years.
nodes.src: Guillermo Algaze, 'The Uruk World System' (1993; 2005); the critique in Gil Stein, 'Rethinking World-Systems: Diasporas, Colonies, and Interaction in Uruk Mesopotamia' (1999).

nodes.label: Uruk and Predynastic Egypt
nodes.full: Late Predynastic Egypt suddenly shows Mesopotamian things: the cylinder seal, recessed 'palace-facade' brick architecture, high-prowed boats, the 'master of animals' gripping two beasts, intertwined serpent-necked creatures — on the Gebel el-Arak knife handle, on painted pottery, in tomb design. The contact was probably indirect, via the Levant or the Red Sea, and it fed into the imagery of Egypt's own emerging kingship before fading.
nodes.src: Rainer Michael Boehmer on the decorated knife-handles; the Egyptian side in the folio egypt-6000bc-3000bc; synthesis in Toby Wilkinson, 'Early Dynastic Egypt' (1999).

nodes.label: The lapis road and the highland trade
nodes.full: Deep-blue lapis lazuli, mined only in the mountains of Badakhshan in northeast Afghanistan, reached Uruk in quantity — passed hand to hand across the Iranian plateau through a chain of intermediary towns. With it came carnelian, chlorite, tin and silver. The routes that carried these stones are the arteries the Uruk expansion tried to tap, and they outlast the expansion by millennia.
nodes.src: Lapis sourcing and the 'trans-Elamite' route in Georgina Herrmann, 'Lapis Lazuli: The Early Phases of its Trade' (Iraq 1968); Daniel Potts, 'Mesopotamian Civilization' (1997).

nodes.label: Susa and the Proto-Elamite answer
nodes.full: Susa, on the plain east of the Tigris, moved in and out of the Uruk orbit — sometimes indistinguishable from a southern Mesopotamian city, sometimes going its own way. Around 3100 BC the Iranian plateau produced 'Proto-Elamite', its own undeciphered script and accounting system, clearly prompted by the Uruk model but built separately. The Uruk world had a rival, not just a periphery.
nodes.src: Proto-Elamite in Robert Englund's 'The State of Decipherment of Proto-Elamite' (2004) and Jacob Dahl's work; Susa's oscillation in Daniel Potts, 'The Archaeology of Elam' (1999).

nodes.label: What moved, and how
nodes.full: Out of the alluvium went cloth, grain, dates, dried fish, worked leather and finished goods, along with the whole administrative toolkit of seal, tablet and standard measure. Back came copper, silver, lead and tin; obsidian, chlorite, alabaster and lapis; cedar and pine; bitumen. River barge and reed boat carried the bulk; donkey caravan and, newly, the ox-wagon took the overland legs.
nodes.src: Trade goods reconstructed from the archaic accounts and from provenance studies in Moorey (1994); transport in Marc Van De Mieroop, 'The Ancient Mesopotamian City' (1997).

nodes.label: The alluvium at its best
nodes.full: The Uruk florescence sat on a landscape near its peak: the rivers still ran in multiple channels reaching most of the plain, the water table and the salt had not yet risen far, and marsh, levee farmland and pasture lay close together. The alluvium could feed a very large population — and briefly did so more densely than anywhere else on earth.
nodes.src: Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); river-channel and marsh landscape in Jennifer Pournelle's geoarchaeology of the Uruk hinterland.

nodes.label: The hyper-urban revolution
nodes.full: Survey of the Uruk countryside shows the villages emptying as the cities grew: by around 3000 BC the great majority of the southern population — on some estimates four in five people — lived inside a walled town, with Uruk alone holding tens of thousands. No other pre-modern society concentrated itself in cities to this degree. The Mesopotamian city was not a market town among farms; it was where almost everyone lived.
nodes.src: Robert Adams & Hans Nissen, 'The Uruk Countryside' (1972); Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981).

nodes.label: The colonial map
nodes.full: At its widest the Uruk network ran from the alluvium up the Euphrates to the foot of the Taurus, along the Tigris past Nineveh, and east over the Zagros passes deep into Iran — planted towns, enclaves in local settlements, and way-stations on the trade roads. It is the first time a southern Mesopotamian order projected itself across so much of the Near East, prefiguring the later empires that would rule the same ground.
nodes.src: Mapped in Guillermo Algaze, 'The Uruk World System' (1993; 2005), and 'Ancient Mesopotamia at the Dawn of Civilization' (2008).

nodes.label: The dry turn at the end
nodes.full: Lake and cave records across West Asia register a shift to drier conditions in the centuries around 3200–3000 BC. Its weight is argued — but the timing coincides with the collapse of the northern colonies, a contraction of rain-fed settlement in the periphery, and the turn of the southern cities toward competing with one another over the shrinking margin of water and land.
nodes.src: Michael Staubwasser & Harvey Weiss, 'Holocene Climate and Cultural Evolution in Late Prehistoric–Early Historic West Asia' (Quaternary Research 2006); its causal role debated.

nodes.label: The urban crowd
nodes.full: To live in Uruk was to be one of tens of thousands, most of them strangers, packed inside a wall, eating grain grown by someone else and issued from a central store. The dense mutual knowledge of the village was gone; in its place came neighbourhoods, institutions, officials, and a daily dependence on the temple household. The city offered specialisation, safety and opportunity, and took ordinary self-sufficiency in exchange.
nodes.src: Marc Van De Mieroop, 'The Ancient Mesopotamian City' (1997); the social texture reconstructed from the archaic administrative record.

nodes.label: The captive and the work gang
nodes.full: Named in the ration lists, worked in gangs under overseers, fed a fixed measure of barley: the dependent labourer is the commonest person in the Uruk archive. Many were bound — the sign for a female slave writes 'woman' plus 'mountain', and the priest-king is shown taking prisoners. The prosperity carved on the Warka Vase rested on people whose names survive only as entries in a payroll of rations.
nodes.src: Ignace Gelb, 'Prisoners of War in Early Mesopotamia' (1973); ration-list labour in 'Archaic Bookkeeping' (1993).

nodes.label: The scribe, a new kind of person
nodes.full: Writing created an occupation that had not existed: the person trained to make and read the marks. The copied sign-lists and practice tablets show an apprenticeship. A scribe could turn a spoken order into a permanent record, check one account against another, and calculate a quota — and so a scribe sat close to power, holding a skill that most officials did not have.
nodes.src: Scribal training in Niek Veldhuis, 'History of the Cuneiform Lexical Tradition' (2014); the social position of the early scribe in Glassner, 'The Invention of Cuneiform' (2003).

nodes.label: Women in the workshops
nodes.full: The textile accounts list workforces overwhelmingly of women and children, spinning and weaving for rations inside the institutions. At the same time women served as priestesses and appear as the 'pigtailed ladies' running workshops on the seals. Whether the move into the city and its managed economy raised or lowered women's standing compared with village life is debated, and the evidence pulls both ways.
nodes.src: Textile-workshop demographics from the archaic and later Ur III accounts; the status debate in Julia Asher-Greve and in Diane Bolger, 'Gender Through Time in the Ancient Near East' (2008).

nodes.label: The body in the first city
nodes.full: The skeletal record for the Uruk period itself is thin — burials are modest and few have been excavated — but the conditions can be read from what surrounds them: a crowded settlement, a diet leaning heavily on rationed barley, animals and people living close, and the parasites and fevers of the marsh. The lavish royal tombs and better-studied populations come a few centuries later, at Early Dynastic Ur.
nodes.src: The scarcity of Uruk-period burials noted in Susan Pollock, 'Ancient Mesopotamia' (1999); regional bioarchaeology in Arkadiusz Sołtysiak's work.
